title: Balanced at Every Node
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree. Call a node even if the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1 (an empty subtree has height 0). Return true if every node in the tree is even, and false otherwise.

It is not enough for the root to be even. An empty tree counts as balanced.

Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child.

examples.why: At the root both sides are 3 levels tall, so the root is even. But node 4 has a left side 2 levels tall (3 → 1) and an empty right side.
Leaves sit at depths 2, 3 and 4, yet every node's two sides differ by at most 1. "All leaves within one level of each other" is a stricter rule than this one.
There is no node that breaks the rule.

constraints: The tree is at most 500 levels deep
hints: Checking the root alone is not enough. What would checking every node naively cost if each check measures two heights from scratch?
You already compute heights bottom-up. A child could tell its parent its height and, at the same time, whether it was itself balanced.
Write height(node) that returns -1 when anything below is unbalanced. If either child returns -1, or |l - r| > 1, return -1; otherwise return 1 + max(l, r).

explain.intuition:
The rule must hold at every node, so the direct approach is: at each node, measure both subtree heights and compare, then recurse into both children. That works, but the bottom of the tree gets measured again for every ancestor above it: O(n · h).

The fix is to measure heights once, bottom-up, and let the comparison ride along. When height(node) has its children's heights l and r, it can check |l − r| ≤ 1 right there. If the check fails, it records the failure on the side: either in an outer flag, or by returning a sentinel like -1 that every ancestor passes straight up. This is the same "return the height, record the answer on the side" shape as finding the longest walk in a tree. A layout engine works the same way: one pass computes each box's size from its children and flags overflow as it goes, instead of re-measuring every subtree from every ancestor.
steps: Compute l = height(node.left); if it is -1, return -1 right away.
Compute r = height(node.right); if it is -1, return -1.
If |l − r| > 1, return -1. Otherwise return 1 + max(l, r).
The tree is balanced exactly when height(root) != -1.
pitfalls: Checking only the root's two heights. The first example is even at the root and uneven one level down.
Using "the shallowest and deepest leaves differ by at most 1". That rejects trees that are balanced by this definition, like the second example.
Mixing up a real height and the failure signal. If you use -1 as the signal, check for it before doing arithmetic with it, or a failed child can look like a normal short one.

solutions.title: Top-down: check every node with fresh heights
solutions.idea: At each node, compute both subtree heights and compare, then check both children the same way. Simple, but heights near the bottom are recomputed once per ancestor.

solutions.title: Bottom-up height with a -1 signal
solutions.idea: One post-order pass. Each call returns its height, or -1 if anything at or below it is uneven; -1 passes straight up to the root.

followups: Return the value of the highest uneven node, or null if there is none.
Given a sorted array, build a tree that passes this check. Why does picking the middle element as the root work?
